Mixed model for repeated measures in a longitudinal Solomon design

Source: R/solomon_mmrm.R
fit_solomon_mmrm.Rd

Analyzes a Solomon four-group design with several posttest occasions by a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM), and estimates the four Solomon contrasts and the pretest effects at each occasion, and the change in pretest sensitization from the first occasion to the last. The model is likelihood-based, so its treatment contrasts are valid when posttests are missing at random, for example when participants drop out depending on their earlier scores (Fitzmaurice et al., 2011, pp. 497, 505). The pretest effects rest instead on the assumption of the pretest center when some pretested participants have no posttest at any occasion (see "Missing posttests and the pretest center" below). Per-occasion analyses of the participants still observed, and unweighted generalized estimating equations, require the stronger assumption that the posttests are missing completely at random (Liang & Zeger, 1986; Fitzmaurice et al., 2011, pp. 358, 498). The section "Limits" states what else the model assumes and where its standard errors are approximate.

Usage

fit_solomon_mmrm(
  y_post,
  treat,
  pretested,
  id,
  occasion,
  y_pre = NULL,
  df = c("kenward-roger", "satterthwaite"),
  conf_level = 0.95,
  data = NULL,
  pretest_center = c("analyzed", "observed")
)

Arguments

y_post

Numeric posttest scores, one per participant and occasion (long format), with NA for missing posttests.

treat

Treatment indicator coded 0/1 (or logical), the same in every row of a participant. Designs with several treatments are not supported; see fit_solomon_glm().

pretested

Pretest indicator coded 0/1 (or logical), the same in every row of a participant.

id

Participant identifier.

occasion

Posttest occasion. A factor keeps its level order; otherwise the sorted unique values are used. An ordered factor is used as unordered, in its level order; the contrasts at each occasion do not depend on how occasion is coded. It must not be missing; a value at an NA level of a factor, as made by addNA(), counts as missing.

y_pre

Optional pretest score, the same in every row of a participant and missing by design for unpretested participants.

df

Degrees of freedom for tests and intervals: "kenward-roger" (default) or "satterthwaite".

conf_level

Confidence level. Default 0.95.

data

Optional data frame. When supplied, the other data arguments are looked up in it first, as bare column names (y_post = post) or as strings (y_post = "post").

pretest_center

With y_pre, the mean pretest at which the pretested groups are compared with the unpretested groups, as in fit_solomon_glm() (issue #135). "analyzed" (the default): the mean pretest of the pretested participants in the model, those with at least one posttest. "observed": the mean of every observed pretest among the pretested participants, each counted once, with or without a posttest at any occasion; the rows of pretested participants with no posttest must be in the data, with y_post missing, or this gives the default. Ignored without y_pre.

Value

An object of class solomon_mmrm, a list with:

  • effects: at each occasion, the four treatment contrasts, ATE (avg over pretest), Pretest x Treatment, Treatment | pretested, and Treatment | unpretested, and the three pretest effects, Pretest effect | control, Pretest effect | treated, and Pretest main effect; then Change in Pretest x Treatment, the change in sensitization from the first occasion to the last. The columns are occasion, contrast, estimate, std.error, statistic (t), df, p.value, conf.low, and conf.high. In the last row, occasion names the two occasions, as in "3 vs 1".

  • conf_level: the confidence level of the intervals.

  • model: the fitted model, an mmrm object.

  • covariance: the covariance structure used.

  • grouped: whether the covariance was estimated separately for pretested and unpretested participants.

  • df_method: the degrees of freedom, "kenward-roger" or "satterthwaite".

  • pretest_mean: the mean pretest at which the pretest is centered, the center used; NA without y_pre.

  • pretest_center, pretest_mean_analyzed, pretest_mean_observed, pretest_n, and pretest_sensitivity: as in fit_solomon_glm(), with each participant counted once. The participants "analyzed" are those with at least one posttest; the tables of pretest_sensitivity are keyed by occasion; its slope holds the pretest slope of each occasion; its attrition counts the participants of each group without any posttest; and its delta is NULL, because no delta line is derived for repeated posttests.

  • pretest_slope: the pretest slope at each occasion, named by occasion; NULL without y_pre.

  • occasions: the posttest occasions, in order.

  • observed: the number of observed posttests in each group, one column for each occasion.

  • excluded: the number of pretested participants left out because their pretest was missing (see Details).

  • pretest (whether pretest scores were supplied) and data (the design indicators of each participant), which solomonR's own functions use.

The effects table, conf_level, and tidy(), which returns the table, are the stable interface of the result; see solomon_output.

Model

The specification follows the example of Mallinckrodt et al. (2008, p. 312), adapted to the Solomon design:

  • Fixed effects. Occasion x Treatment x Pretested, all categorical.

  • Pretest adjustment. The pretest enters as in fit_solomon_glm(): in the pretested groups, the score minus the mean pretest of the pretested participants in the model (each counted once; returned as pretest_mean; with pretest_center = "observed", the mean of every observed pretest among the pretested participants, with or without a posttest), and 0 in the unpretested groups, with a separate slope at each occasion ("a full interaction of the covariate with time", p. 312). Pretests absent by design are never imputed.

  • Pretest effects. At each occasion, the pretest effects among controls, among treated participants, and their average compare pretested and unpretested participants at that mean pretest, as described in the section "The pretest effect" of fit_solomon_glm(). Pretest effects may fade with time (Entwisle, 1961, p. 610), and these estimates show whether they do. Their standard errors include the sampling variance of the mean pretest, s^2 / n for n pretested participants, times the square of that occasion's pretest slope, and their degrees of freedom combine those of the contrast with n - 1 by the Welch-Satterthwaite formula (Satterthwaite, 1946; Welch, 1947). The pretest effects were not part of the validation study below.

  • Missing posttests and the pretest center. As in fit_solomon_glm() (see its section "The pretest effect when posttests are missing"), the pretest effects depend on the mean pretest at which they are evaluated when some pretested participants have no posttest at any occasion; pretest_center chooses it, and "observed" needs those participants' rows, with y_post missing. At each occasion, the pretest effects at the two centers differ by that occasion's pretest slope times the difference between the two means. Which center is right depends on who was lost before the first posttest. When all four groups lose participants alike by their baseline, the default is unbiased, and "observed" is off by that difference. When only the pretested groups lose them by their pretest, and the unpretested groups' losses are unrelated to baseline, "observed" is unbiased, and the default is off by it (the decision record posted on issue #135, section 1). A participant with a posttest at any occasion is analyzed, so dropout after the first occasion leaves the two centers equal. Neither center protects the later occasions when dropout depends on baseline beyond the earlier posttests: the unpretested groups' model cannot see the baseline, so their later posttests are not missing at random given what it includes. In a check of this (tools/pretest-center-check.R, part 5: 40 data sets of 1,500 participants per group, no effects, two occasions, a third of the second posttests lost with probability plogis(-1 - 1.5 * x) in every group, x the baseline), the pretest main effect was unbiased at the first occasion (0.000, Monte Carlo standard error 0.004) and biased at the second by -0.067 (0.005) at either center. When dropout depended on the first posttest instead, both occasions were unbiased (-0.005 and -0.002). When a third of the participants had no posttest at all, lost by baseline in every group, the default was unbiased and "observed" biased by -0.18 at both occasions; when only the pretested groups lost them by baseline, and the unpretested at random, the reverse held (+0.18 at the default). It is a check, not a simulation study.

  • Covariance. Unstructured within participant, estimated by restricted maximum likelihood (Laird & Ware, 1982). With a pretest, it is estimated separately for pretested and unpretested participants: the pretest adjustment makes the residual covariance conditional on the pretest in the pretested groups only, so a single shared matrix would be misspecified. The treated and the control group of a pretest condition share one matrix; see "Limits".

  • Fallback. If the unstructured model does not converge, the heterogeneous Toeplitz, heterogeneous AR(1), and heterogeneous compound symmetry structures are fitted, and the converged one with the smallest AIC is used (Mallinckrodt et al., 2008, p. 312). The output names the structure used. "Limits" says what changes after a fallback.

  • Inference. t tests and intervals with Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom and adjusted covariance (Kenward & Roger, 1997, as cited in Fitzmaurice et al., 2011, p. 101), as Mallinckrodt et al. (2008, p. 312) specify, or with Satterthwaite (1946) degrees of freedom. The Kenward-Roger adjustment depends on how the covariance is parameterized. It is computed in its linear form (mmrm's "Kenward-Roger-Linear"), which leaves out the term of the adjustment that holds the second derivatives of the covariance matrix with respect to its parameters (Sabanes Bove et al., 2026). With the unstructured matrix and its own elements as the parameters, that term is zero, and the computation reproduces SAS PROC MIXED. This holds for the unstructured matrix only, not after a fallback (see "Limits"). Fitzmaurice et al. (2011, p. 101) note that the small-sample properties of both approximations in longitudinal models "have not been extensively studied"; the simulation study posted on issue #57 compares them in Solomon designs.

The model is fitted with the mmrm package (Sabanes Bove et al., 2026), version 0.3.13 or later, which must be installed.

A pretested participant with no pretest score in any row is excluded, with a warning, as missing_pretest = "drop" excludes them in fit_solomon_glm(), and the print says how many and why. For the pretest effects, that assumes that in each pretested group those without a pretest would have had the same mean posttests as those with one; when their loss relates to baseline, the pretest effects are biased (see "Pretested participants without a pretest" in fit_solomon_glm()). Keeping them by the missing-indicator method, as missing_pretest = "indicator" does there, waits for an amendment to the protocol of issue #57.

Limits

These limits come from the model and from the literature on it. They do not depend on the results of a simulation study.

  • Dropout that depends on scores. The standard errors rest on the expected information, as mmrm and SAS PROC MIXED compute it, with either choice of df. Kenward and Molenberghs (1998) show that when dropout depends on the scores observed before it, the mean and the covariance parameters of the normal model are no longer orthogonal (p. 242): their estimates are correlated however large the sample. Such standard errors can then be wrong at any sample size, and Kenward and Molenberghs recommend the observed information instead (pp. 238–239, 247). In the simulations of Maruo et al. (2020, Table 1), with 200 participants per arm, three occasions, maximum likelihood, and dropout that depended on the previous score, the usual standard error of the treatment difference at the last occasion was 4% to 5% too small with 20% of the last scores missing, and 13% to 17% too small with 40%, when each arm had its own unstructured matrix. When the arms rightly shared one matrix, it was within 2% of the right value. With a pretest in the model, a treatment contrast compares two groups that share a matrix, and a pretest effect compares two groups whose matrices are estimated separately. The limit therefore bears on the pretest effects: under such dropout their standard errors can be too small. The function does not offer standard errors from the observed information. The printed output of a fit with a pretest and missing posttests carries a note.

  • One covariance matrix for both arms. The model assumes that the treated and the control group of a pretest condition have the same covariance matrix. With one unstructured matrix for both arms and the Kenward-Roger method, Gosho and Maruo (2018) found that intervals for the treatment effect covered too rarely when the arm with more dropout had the larger variance, and that the estimate was biased as well when the arms' correlations also differed. The covariance estimator of Mancl and DeRouen (2001, as cited in Gosho & Maruo, 2018) did better in the first case, and a matrix for each arm in the second. The function offers neither.

  • After a fallback. The fallback structures are not linear in their parameters. For such structures, the default Kenward-Roger adjustment of SAS PROC MIXED includes the second-derivative term, which can shrink the standard errors and depends on the parameterization; its FIRSTORDER option leaves the term out (SAS Institute Inc., 2009). This function always leaves it out, so after a fallback it gives the first-order form of the adjustment, not the default of SAS. The structure is also chosen by AIC, which is unreliable in small samples. With 10 participants in two groups and five occasions, AIC chose the true structure, when that was simpler than the unstructured one, in 27% to 73% of complete samples and in 20% to 66% of samples with dropouts (Skene & Kenward, 2010, Table II). In the simulations of Gomez et al. (2005), Kenward-Roger tests had Type I error rates above the nominal level whenever the structure was chosen by AIC or BIC. The inference after a fallback has not been evaluated for this function: in the simulation study below, the unstructured model converged in every replication.

  • Outcomes that are not normal. The model assumes normal residuals, and the simulation study below drew normal outcomes. From simulations with 30 to 42 participants in three groups, Arnau et al. (2012) conclude that Kenward-Roger tests are compromised when the outcome is moderately skewed, as a log-normal outcome is, most of all for the effect of time, and that they hold up when it is normal or only slightly skewed.

Validation

A simulation study under a protocol posted on issue #57 before any run (12 scenarios, 2,000 replications each; see the article "Longitudinal Designs: Validating the Repeated-Measures Analysis") generated monotone dropout that depended on the last posttest. With 30 to 120 participants per group:

  • Coverage and Type I error. With Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom, 95% intervals covered from 0.937 to 0.962 of the time, and Type I error where the true value was zero ranged from 0.041 to 0.0615. Satterthwaite degrees of freedom performed alike.

  • Bias. The contrasts were unbiased; the largest bias was 0.029 SD.

  • Normal reference distribution. It gave coverage as low as 0.935 at 30 per group.

  • Shared covariance. A covariance shared by all four groups misstated the standard errors by up to 12% for the unpretested contrasts and 17% for the pretested ones.

  • Complete-case analyses. Per-occasion analyses of the participants still observed were biased by up to 0.09 SD at the last occasion.

Lifecycle

Experimental. The study's pre-specified rule for choosing the default degrees of freedom, every tolerance met in 90% of cells and in every cell with 60 or more per group, was not met by either approximation (145 of 156 cells each; 97 and 96 of 104), although Monte Carlo error alone makes the second part unlikely to be met even by a correctly calibrated method. Kenward-Roger remains the default, as Mallinckrodt et al. (2008) specify.

See also

fit_solomon_glm() for a single posttest occasion; jordaan2014 and the article "Worked Example: Repeated Posttests" for a published study with three posttest occasions.

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("mmrm", quietly = TRUE) && utils::packageVersion("mmrm") >= "0.3.13") {
  # Three posttest occasions for the example participants, with dropout.
  set.seed(57)
  d <- solomon_example
  d$id <- seq_len(nrow(d))
  long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(t) {
    x <- d
    x$occasion <- t
    x$y_post <- d$y_post - 2 * (t - 1) + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 4)
    x
  }))
  long$y_post[long$occasion == 3 & runif(nrow(long)) < 0.3] <- NA
  fit_solomon_mmrm(y_post, treat, pretested, id, occasion, y_pre, data = long)
}
